# SK5041 — The key-derivation salt is fixed at compile time

<!-- Generated from Rules/Rikarin.Skala.Rules.Metadata/rules.json. Do not edit. -->

PBKDF2 with a hard-coded salt derives the same key from the same password on every machine, which is what a salt exists to prevent.

| | |
|---|---|
| Category | Security |
| Default severity | error |
| Scope | Semantic |
| Needs a compilation | yes |
| Fix | no |
| Language version floor | — |
| Since | 2.0 |
| Supersedes | S2053 |

## Why

A salt is what stops one unit of work from breaking many credentials. It is not a secret and it does not have to be — it has to be *different for every credential*, so that an attacker who takes the store cannot precompute anything reusable. Fix it, and the property is gone in both directions: a rainbow table built once against that one salt breaks every password in the store at once, and any two users who chose the same password have visibly identical derived keys, so the store leaks who shares a password with whom before anything is even cracked. Draw sixteen bytes from `RandomNumberGenerator.GetBytes(16)` per credential and store them beside the derived key; that is what the verifying side reads back. ⚠ There is no fix. The edit changes what a stored credential record contains, so every password already written becomes unverifiable by the new code — the migration is to re-derive on next successful sign-in, which is a change to the program's behaviour rather than to its text. That is the same call `SK5005` and `SK5020` make.

## Example

Instead of:

```csharp
static readonly byte[] Salt = { 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8 };

byte[] Derive(string password) =>
    Rfc2898DeriveBytes.Pbkdf2(password, Salt, 600_000, HashAlgorithmName.SHA256, 32);
```

Write:

```csharp
(byte[] Salt, byte[] Key) Derive(string password) {
    var salt = RandomNumberGenerator.GetBytes(16);
    return (salt, Rfc2898DeriveBytes.Pbkdf2(password, salt, 600_000, HashAlgorithmName.SHA256, 32));
}
```

## When it does not fire

⚠ **Issue #139 arrived as two halves and only this one survived.** The fast-hash half — a password stored under a general-purpose digest — is refuted: deciding that a hash is being applied to a *password* means reading identifier names, which is the judgement that cut `SK5008` and half of `SK5005`, and the type test cannot stand in for it because `HashAlgorithm` is the base class for **checksums**, with CRC32, xxHash and Murmur deriving from it for the streaming plumbing. This half needs neither, because the receiver is a key-derivation function whose own first parameter the BCL names `password` — the API asserts what the input is, so the rule does not guess. ⚠ **Measured unhosted, and the measurement published on #139 was wrong in one particular that is worth correcting.** On a plain `net10.0` project outside this repository under `AnalysisMode=All` with every `CA5xxx` raised to `warning`, `CA5387` **does** fire on a 100-iteration `Rfc2898DeriveBytes`, where #139 recorded it producing nothing — but it fires on the **iteration count** and nothing else. It fired on a call whose salt was a perfectly good `byte[]` parameter, and it was silent on a 100 000-iteration derivation with a hard-coded eight-byte salt and on a 100 000-iteration `Pbkdf2` with an all-zero salt. `CA5379` looks only at the hash algorithm. So nothing in the SDK reports a constant salt at any iteration count, and the zero is *shape present and declined* — a planted `DataSet.ReadXml` in the same file fired `CA2351` and `CA5366`. ⚠ **`HKDF` is deliberately not a receiver, and it is the false positive this rule exists to avoid.** RFC 5869 says HKDF's salt is optional and *may be fixed and public*: it extracts from high-entropy input keying material rather than from a password, and a protocol that pins its salt so both ends derive the same key is using it exactly as specified. That is the protocol-fixed derivation shape, and it is excluded by receiver rather than by a judgement about intent. PBKDF2 is the opposite case — it is *defined* for passwords, and the same fixed salt there is the defect. ⚠ **Test methods are exempt, and here the exemption is load-bearing rather than a courtesy: RFC 6070's PBKDF2 test vectors specify the salt as the literal string `"salt"`.** Without it this rule would fail the build of every crypto library that checks itself against the standard's own vectors, at `error` severity — which is how a reviewer learns to skim past every security finding a tool makes. ⚠ **The verifying side is silent by construction, and that is the design.** Checking a password re-derives with the salt stored alongside the hash, which is a variable, a parameter or a field read from a record — and nothing here resolves any of those. So the rule reports the code that *creates* a bad credential and stays quiet on the code that reads it back, the same asymmetry `SK5020` draws between `CreateEncryptor` and `CreateDecryptor`. ⚠ **Only a constant written at the call.** `var salt = new byte[16]; RandomNumberGenerator.Fill(salt);` is how correct code is written and a rule that followed `salt` to its declaration would report it, so the constant must be at the argument itself or be the initialiser of a field holding an explicit list of literals. `Rfc2898DeriveBytes(password, saltSize)` generates its own salt and has no `salt` parameter, so it is silent without being named. ⚠ **`SYSLIB0060` already marks every `Rfc2898DeriveBytes` constructor obsolete on by default**, so that half of the population is legacy code; the static `Pbkdf2` overloads carry no obsoletion and are where a fixed salt gets written today, which is why both are covered. ⚠ **The reference trees prove nothing here and the zero is reported as such**: not one of the 4 459 files under `Testing/corpus` mentions `System.Security.Cryptography`, so a corpus zero is *shape absent* rather than *correctly declined*, and the evidence for this rule is its fixtures plus the sabotage set.
